summary:
AstroHealth is a web-based prototype designed to support astronaut health monitoring during space missions. We developed a React interface, a Node.js backend, and a FastAPI service integrating 16 machine-learning models. The platform covers radiation exposure, psychological wellbeing, gravity-related health effects, nutrition, and respiration.

Users submit health measurements, receive model-generated assessments, and access reports stored in a database. The platform also includes a complete PHQ-9 screening questionnaire, cognitive practice puzzles, and saved astronaut profiles that simplify repeated assessments.

AstroHealth addresses the challenge of bringing multiple aspects of astronaut health into one accessible system. By organizing measurements and assessment results in a consistent workflow, it helps users review health information and supports further investigation of potential concerns.

This is important because space missions expose astronauts to interconnected physical and psychological stressors while access to medical resources is limited. The current models are research prototypes trained on synthetic or rule-labeled data; their outputs support demonstration and further development, rather than clinical diagnosis.
details:
AstroHealth is a web-based health-monitoring prototype designed to bring astronaut health information into one accessible platform. It covers five areas: radiation exposure, psychological wellbeing, gravity-related health effects, nutrition, and respiration.

How it works

Users enter measurements through forms organized by assessment type. Saved astronaut and mission details are added automatically, reducing repetitive data entry. The Node.js backend validates each submission and sends it to a FastAPI service containing 16 machine-learning models. The service processes the available measurements and returns predictions, identifying specialist assessments that cannot run because required inputs are missing. The backend then saves the submitted measurements and model outputs together in MongoDB and returns the complete report to the user.

The platform also includes a nine-question PHQ-9 screening questionnaire with automatic scoring and cognitive practice puzzles covering memory, logic, patterns, mathematics, words, and spatial reasoning. Screening results and puzzle scores are presented separately from model predictions.

Benefits and intended impact

AstroHealth reduces fragmented recordkeeping by combining multiple health domains in a consistent assessment and reporting workflow. Saved reports provide a foundation for reviewing measurements over time and developing future monitoring capabilities.

Our intended impact is to demonstrate how an integrated digital platform could support health-information management during missions where medical resources and specialist access are limited. The system is intended to support further research and development, rather than replace professional medical judgment.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React, JavaScript, Tailwind CSS, and Vite.
  • Backend: Node.js and Express.
  • Model service: Python, FastAPI, PyTorch, and NumPy.
  • Database: MongoDB.
  • Deployment and collaboration: Vercel, Git, and GitHub.

The prototype runs through a browser and uses CPU-based inference. It currently accepts manually entered measurements and does not require specialized hardware or connected sensors.

Creativity and design considerations

The creative approach combines physical-health assessments, psychological screening, and cognitive practice within a mission-oriented interface. Rather than presenting isolated predictions, the platform connects measurements, astronaut context, model results, and saved reports in one workflow.

We considered input consistency, missing measurements, mobile usability, error recovery, prevention of duplicate submissions, deployment constraints, and clear communication of model limitations. Sensitive database credentials are stored in deployment environment variables rather than source code.

The current models were trained on synthetic or rule-labeled data and have not been clinically validated. Clinical validation, authentication, stronger access controls, and testing under realistic mission conditions would be necessary before operational use.
